title: This Brainless Organism Redesigned Tokyo's Entire Rail Network
description:
A single-celled slime mold with no brain and no nervous system can solve a maze -- and when researchers tested it on a bigger problem, it built something remarkably close to Tokyo's actual rail network.

#shorts #sciencefacts #biology #didyouknow
sources: Nakagaki et al., Nature (2000), "Maze-solving by an amoeboid organism"
Tero et al., Science (2010), "Rules for Biologically Inspired Adaptive Network Design"
ScienceDaily's "Slime design mimics Tokyo's rail system"
National Geographic's coverage of the Tokyo rail slime mold study

scenes.text: There's a living organism with no brain, no neurons, not even a single nervous system cell -- and it can still solve a maze.

In 2000, researchers placed this slime mold in a maze with food at both ends. Within hours, it had pulled back from every dead end and connected both food sources along the single shortest path through the maze.

A decade later, the same researchers tried something far bigger. They placed oat flakes on a map in the exact positions of Tokyo's major cities, and let the slime mold grow its own network connecting them.
What it built was remarkably close to Tokyo's actual rail system -- built by professional engineers over decades -- in both efficiency and total cost.
It does all this with one simple rule: the more a path gets used, the stronger it grows. The less it's used, the more it shrinks away on its own.
It wasn't flawless, though. The real Tokyo rail network still beat it on one measure -- losing a single connection broke apart the slime mold's version more often than it did the real one.
Would you have guessed a brainless organism could design something close to a real transit system?
